The conversion plant would require approximately 1,000 acres for facilities plus additional acreage for access roads, pipelines, and possible rail spur.
Either process would require a cooling pond or cooling towers, most likely of the wet design. Water requirements could be reduced by using "dry cooling" or other forms of recirculation. Provision would have to be made for disposing of discharge from exhaust scrubbers and ash from the combustion process. Conceivably both products could be sluiced to a sealed storage reservoir, although ash could be buried in the mine pit.
A coal gasification facility using the CO<sub>2</sub> Acceptor Process and the electric power generation process are described in detail in "Energy Alternatives: A Comparative Analysis", which was published jointly by the Council on Environmental Quality and several other federal agencies. The publication has been distributed to appropriate Federal agencies and libraries, and is also available from the Superintendent of Documents, U.S. Government Printing Office, Washington D.C. 20402.
RELATED FEDERAL ACTIONS
The Bureau of Indian Affairs has a trust responsibility over the Indian coal rights. It is responsible for ensuring that applicable environmental laws and regulations are adhered to with regard to the Westmoreland Resources lease area. Bureau of Indian Affairs leases are written in accordance with the Omnibus Indian Mineral Leasing Act of 1938. By its terms "unallotted lands within any Indian Reservation or lands owned by any Indian Tribe under federal jurisdiction, could be leased for mining purposes.......for terms not to exceed ten years and as long thereafter as minerals are produced in paying quantities".
